strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing 3D affordance datasets are all derived from a single 23-class asset source with limited scale and often flawed heatmaps (well-illustrated in Fig. 4); the paper convincingly motivates need for a larger, more diverse, open-vocabulary resource.

Affogato-Engine is a scalable, fully automated pipeline (VLM query generation + pointing model + SAM + multi-view voting) that produces a genuinely large-scale (150K objects, 750K query-heatmap pairs) dataset spanning both 3D and 2D modalities from a shared source, which is a useful unification not previously offered.

Reasonably careful quality control: a held-out human-evaluated and refined test split, three-tier quality rating, and quantitative coverage/diversity comparisons against LASO give some assurance of annotation reliability.

Extensive empirical validation: cross-dataset generalization (LASO vs Affogato), cross-category open-vocabulary generalization within Affogato, zero-shot and fine-tuned 2D evaluation on AGD20K against multiple strong baselines (LISA, M2SA, OOAL, LOCATE, etc.), plus supplementary ablations (background augmentation, partial-view robustness) — the experimental scope is broad for a dataset paper.

Simple, modality-shared Espresso architecture with frozen pretrained encoders (PartField, DINOv2, CLIP) is easy to reproduce and demonstrates that the dataset itself, rather than architectural novelty, drives the improvements, supporting the claimed contribution type (dataset/benchmark).
Plan to publicly release the dataset and generation engine increases potential community impact and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Automated annotation quality is only spot-checked on a small subset (1K objects / 5K pairs) relative to the full 150K/750K dataset, and ~27.7% of sampled pairs were rated 'ok' or 'not good'; no inter-annotator agreement or more systematic noise-quantification is reported, leaving open how much residual noise affects the bulk of training data.

The proposed coverage/diversity metrics (KL divergence and union coverage) are not obviously calibrated against annotation correctness — heatmaps that are simply more diffuse/noisy could trivially score higher on both metrics, so the claimed 'superior diversity' over LASO is not fully convincing without a quality-normalized analysis.

Cross-dataset comparisons (Table 2) between LASO and Affogato use the same absolute metrics (aIoU, AUC, SIM) despite acknowledging that annotation protocols/scales differ enough to make MAE unreliable; it is unclear why the other metrics are assumed robust to the same distributional differences.

Missing comparisons with more recent/stronger 3D affordance baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., 3D-AffordanceLLM, SeqAfford), limiting the assessment of how Espresso and Affogato compare to current state of the art beyond OpenAD and PointRefer.
Licensing, attribution, and potential biases of the underlying Objaverse web-crawled assets are not discussed, which is relevant given the dataset's intended public release.

Limited discussion of how pipeline failure modes (misidentified object categories, SAM edge bias, occluded target parts) quantitatively propagate into downstream model performance, beyond qualitative examples in the appendix.

The Espresso architecture itself is a fairly direct combination of existing components (PartField/DINOv2/CLIP encoders with a standard cross-attention mask decoder), so algorithmic novelty is minimal — acceptable for a dataset-centric contribution but should be more explicitly framed as such rather than presented as a joint contribution.

strengths: Substantial scale increase over prior 3D affordance datasets (150K instances vs. ~23K for prior work), spanning both 3D and 2D modalities with a unified pipeline.

Open-vocabulary text queries generated via VLMs remove reliance on fixed affordance/object taxonomies used by all prior 3D affordance benchmarks, which is a meaningful step for generalization research.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: in-dataset vs. cross-dataset comparisons (LASO vs. Affogato), cross-category open-vocabulary generalization within Affogato, and zero-shot/fine-tuned 2D evaluation against strong LLM-based and affordance-specific baselines on AGD20K.

The Espresso baseline (frozen part-aware 3D/2D encoders + text-conditioned cross-attention decoder) is simple, and the paper shows it is competitive or superior to more complex existing methods, supporting the claim that the dataset itself provides strong transferable supervision.

Useful qualitative and quantitative analysis of failure modes of existing datasets (annotation mismatch, incomplete coverage, low point-cloud resolution) and of the proposed pipeline's own error modes, along with a human-verified test split and an additional partial-view (Affogato-Partial) benchmark variant.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is only moderate for a paper whose entire value proposition is annotation quality/scale: only 72.3% of a small evaluated subset (5K pairs from 1K of the 150K objects) was rated "good," and 15.4% "not good"; no inter-annotator agreement or definition of "domain expert" is reported, making it hard to gauge true noise levels in the ~145K objects not manually checked.

The annotation pipeline chains together three imperfect foundation models (Gemma3 for queries, Molmo for points, SAM for masks); known biases of each (VLM misclassification, Molmo's cross-view inconsistency, SAM's edge bias) compound, and the paper's own failure-mode analysis in the appendix suggests these are not rare, yet no rigorous precision/recall against a larger human-verified gold set is reported to quantify the actual annotation error rate.

Diversity/coverage claims rely on somewhat arbitrary, self-selected thresholds (frequency >10 for object classes, >100 for affordances) and a self-referential diversity metric (pairwise KL divergence between the model's own multiple noisy heatmaps), which do not clearly establish that the annotations are semantically more correct than prior datasets, only that they are more numerous/varied — variety could partly reflect VLM noise/hallucination rather than genuine semantic diversity.

Absolute performance of the proposed baseline remains low in several settings (e.g., aIoU of 0.136 as the best in-dataset result in Table 2, 0.046 under cross-category evaluation in Table 3), raising questions about the practical utility of the benchmark/model despite favorable relative comparisons to weaker baselines.

Selective metric emphasis: MAE results that contradict the paper's generalization narrative (e.g., large increases when transferring from Affogato) are downplayed post hoc as "less reliable," which reads as a rationalization chosen after observing unfavorable results rather than a pre-registered evaluation choice.

The core technical contribution beyond the dataset is limited — Espresso is a straightforward combination of existing pretrained encoders (PartField, DINOv2, CLIP-text) with a standard cross-attention mask-decoder design already used in prior segmentation works, so novelty rests almost entirely on the automated data pipeline, which itself is largely an application of existing off-the-shelf VLMs/SAM rather than a new method.

Limited discussion of licensing/provenance of the web-crawled Objaverse assets and downstream redistribution implications for such a large automatically-generated dataset, and no reported per-subset train/val/test statistics beyond the test-split construction procedure.

strengths: Introduces by far the largest and most diverse open-vocabulary affordance dataset (150K 3D objects, 750K query-heatmap pairs) spanning >450 object classes and >350 affordance types, a substantial leap over prior 3D affordance datasets that are all derived from the same 23-category PartNet source.

The Affogato-Engine annotation pipeline (Gemma3 for query generation, Molmo for pointing, SAM for mask decoding, multi-view voting for 3D aggregation) is a sensible, scalable design that requires no manual labeling for the bulk of the data, with a human-verified/refined test split adding reliability.

The paper provides a genuinely convincing empirical case for the dataset's value: cross-dataset generalization experiments (LASO vs. Affogato), cross-category open-vocabulary generalization (Daily-Used vs. Furnitures), and 2D zero-shot/fine-tuned transfer to AGD20K all consistently show that Affogato-trained models generalize better and/or outperform prior state of the art.

Good qualitative analysis contrasting Affogato annotations with known weaknesses of 3D AffordanceNet-derived datasets (annotation mismatch, incomplete coverage, low point-cloud resolution), supported by a quantitative coverage/diversity metric.

The Espresso baseline architecture is simple and reasonably justified (frozen part-aware/vision-language backbones with a lightweight text-conditioned heatmap decoder), and is shown to be effective across both 2D and 3D modalities with a shared design philosophy, which is a nice unifying contribution.

Extensive supplementary analyses (Affogato-Partial for occluded/partial-view evaluation, background augmentation ablation, human vs. engine annotation comparison, failure-mode analysis) show good scientific diligence and strengthen reproducibility.
Dataset and presumably code are shared publicly, aiding reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: Annotation noise remains substantial: only the 5K test-split pairs are human-verified/refined, while 15.4% of a sampled evaluation set was rated 'not good' overall — the bulk of the 150K training instances still contains this level of unverified noise, which is not deeply analyzed for its downstream effect on model quality.

Because Affogato-Engine relies on SAM (known to be edge/boundary biased) and Molmo pointing, and because Gemma3 can misidentify object categories, there is a compounding annotation risk that is acknowledged but not quantitatively bounded (e.g., no ablation isolating engine-stage error contributions).

Absolute performance of Espresso and baselines on the Affogato benchmark remains fairly low in absolute terms (e.g., aIoU around 0.1–0.2), and the paper does not thoroughly discuss why the task remains this hard on its own benchmark or what upper bound might be expected from the annotation quality itself.

The Espresso architecture is largely a straightforward assembly of existing pretrained components (PartField, DINOv2, CLIP text encoder, standard cross-attention mask decoder); the algorithmic contribution is modest and mainly serves to validate the dataset, which is appropriate for a datasets-focused paper but is somewhat oversold as a co-equal contribution in the abstract/intro.

Direct quantitative comparison against more recent, closely related baselines discussed at length in Related Work (e.g., 3D-AffordanceLLM, SeqAfford) is missing; only OpenAD and PointRefer are used as 3D baselines, leaving open how Affogato-trained simple models compare to more sophisticated LLM-based 3D affordance approaches.

The dataset is built entirely on Objaverse synthetic/web-crawled 3D assets without real backgrounds or scene context; the sim-to-real bridging strategy (random background compositing) is a simple heuristic whose robustness to real-world clutter, occlusion, and multi-object scenes is only lightly explored (acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically stress-tested beyond AGD20K).

MAE results behave counterintuitively across cross-dataset experiments and are explained post hoc as a metric artifact rather than analyzed with a more robust/normalized alternative, which slightly weakens the rigor of the generalization claims.

strengths: Addresses a genuine bottleneck in affordance grounding research: the paper builds Affogato-750K, a dataset that is an order of magnitude larger and far more category-diverse than any prior 3D or 2D affordance dataset, using a fully automated multi-foundation-model pipeline (Gemma3 + Molmo + MobileSAM) with multi-view aggregation.
Careful evaluation methodology: the authors include a human-verified 5K test split with documented failure-mode analysis (84.8% success rate) and quantify heatmap coverage/diversity against LASO.

The Espresso-3D/2D models are deliberately designed as minimal, symmetric baselines to isolate the contribution of the dataset from architecture choices, which is a thoughtful experimental design decision that improves the strength of the causal claim ('pretraining data helps, not model tricks').

Extensive ablations/analyses beyond the main tables: held-out category filtering to rule out train/test leakage, pretraining-scale ablation showing monotonic gains, cross-domain asymmetry analysis attributing the gap to training volume vs. class coverage, synthetic-to-real generalization on Open-X-Embodiment robot scenes, and qualitative pipeline-stage breakdowns.

Gains from Affogato-750K pretraining are shown to transfer to prior methods (OpenAD, PointRefer, AffordanceNet) and not just to the authors' own model, supporting the claim of broad, architecture-agnostic transferability.
Good reproducibility details in the appendix (compute, hyperparameters, prompts, model checkpoints) and dataset release intent.
weaknesses: The pipeline still has a non-trivial ~15% annotation failure rate; although mitigated by human-verified test data, the training set of 750K annotations is not human-checked, so noise/bias from Molmo/MobileSAM/Gemma3 (e.g., systematic edge bias, shape-only guesses without CoT) is baked into the primary training resource, and no downstream ablation isolates the effect of this noise level.

Reported gains from pretraining are sometimes modest or inconsistent: PointRefer degrades on the LASO seen split after pretraining (20.2 vs 20.8 aIoU) and Espresso-3D shows mixed AUC/MAE changes, undermining the 'consistent and substantial' framing in places.

Diversity/category-count claims (e.g., '>450 classes', '>350 affordances') rely on Gemma3's own predictions with an arbitrary frequency threshold (10/100), which is a somewhat self-referential and possibly inflated measure of true open-vocabulary diversity rather than an independently validated taxonomy.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix fundamentally different dataset construction paradigms (manual vs. automated), and the paper does not have a matched-scale/matched-category ablation against, e.g., 2HandedAfforder or RAGNet at comparable data volume to isolate whether gains stem from scale, diversity, or the specific pipeline design.

The dataset is Objaverse-derived and background-free by construction (acknowledged as a limitation), restricting realism; the synthetic-to-real generalization experiment is qualitative/illustrative (Figure 7) rather than quantitatively benchmarked on a real dataset with ground truth.

The cross-domain evaluation (Table 3) shows fairly low absolute performance (e.g., aIoU as low as 3-4 for OpenAD, 13.6 for the best model in-domain), suggesting the benchmark itself still has significant headroom and the practical utility of current models trained on it is limited despite improvements over baselines.

Novelty in the modeling contribution (Espresso) is limited by design—the authors explicitly state it recombines existing pretrained encoders and a standard cross-attention decoder for minimalism, meaning the paper's contribution is essentially entirely the dataset/pipeline rather than any new algorithmic or architectural advance, which is fine given the declared type but should be assessed accordingly rather than as a methods paper.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in affordance grounding research — the scarcity of open-vocabulary annotations — with a fully automated pipeline that avoids costly manual labeling and scales to 150K objects/750K annotations, a substantial increase in category diversity over prior 3D (23 classes) and 2D (up to ~300 classes) datasets.

The evaluation protocol is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: a 5K human-verified test split with documented failure-mode analysis (Fig. 4), ablations on pretraining scale (Table A3), held-out category filtering to rule out label leakage (Table 5), cross-domain asymmetry analysis (Table A4), and background augmentation ablation (Table A1).

The design of Espresso-3D/2D as a deliberately minimal, architecturally symmetric baseline is a sound methodological choice for isolating the dataset's contribution from confounds introduced by heterogeneous prior architectures.

Pretraining on Affogato-750K is shown to transfer to existing baseline methods (OpenAD, PointRefer, AffordanceNet) and not just to the authors' own model, which somewhat supports the claim of general-purpose transferable supervision.

Demonstrated zero-shot transfer to real-world, cluttered robot manipulation scenes (Open X-Embodiment) despite training purely on synthetic Objaverse renderings, which is a meaningful signal of practical applicability.
weaknesses: The annotation pipeline's own reported success rate is only 84.8% on the (arguably easier, curated) verification sample; this means a non-trivial fraction of the 745K non-test-split training annotations are likely noisy (wrong points, mislabeled objects, SAM edge-bias merges), and there is no quantification of how this noise affects downstream training beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.

The dataset's headline diversity statistics (>450 object classes, >350 affordances) are themselves derived from Gemma3 predictions — the same model used to generate the annotations — creating a degree of circularity in validating the dataset's core selling point (category coverage) rather than an independent audit.

Gains from Affogato-750K pretraining are inconsistent and sometimes marginal or negative for prior methods: PointRefer degrades on the LASO seen split (20.2 vs 20.8 aIoU) after pretraining, and OpenAD's unseen improvement is only +0.9 aIoU, undercutting the claim of "substantial and consistent" benefit stated in the abstract/text.

Absolute performance on the paper's own Affogato-750K test split is very low even for the best model (13.6 aIoU in-domain, 4.6 aIoU in the harder cross-domain direction), which is presented as evidence of "headroom" but could equally indicate that the benchmark's automatically generated ground truth is too noisy/ambiguous for reliable quantitative evaluation, especially since evaluation ground truth itself derives from the same imperfect pipeline (only 5K of it human-corrected).

The technical contribution of Espresso is intentionally minimal (assembling existing pretrained encoders — PartField, DINOv2, CLIP, Recap-CLIP — with a standard cross-attention decoder), which is reasonable given the stated goal of isolating dataset effects, but leaves little independent algorithmic novelty; the paper's contribution is almost entirely the dataset/pipeline, and the paper should be judged primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than an algorithmic one.

Coverage/diversity is quantitatively compared only against LASO (Table in Fig. 3d), not against other 2D or 3D datasets in Table 1, weakening the strength of the diversity claims relative to the full related-work landscape.

Limited discussion of the licensing/provenance implications of building a large training corpus from web-crawled Objaverse assets, and no discussion of downstream safety/societal risks of deploying noisy, automatically-generated affordance predictions in embodied/robotic systems where incorrect contact-point predictions could cause physical harm.

strengths: Introduces Affogato-750K, by far the largest and most category-diverse affordance grounding dataset (750K annotations, 150K 3D objects, >450 object classes, >350 affordance classes), substantially exceeding prior datasets in both scale and open-vocabulary coverage (Table 1).

The fully automated annotation pipeline (Gemma3 query generation -> Molmo pointing -> MobileSAM segmentation -> multi-view 3D aggregation) is well-motivated and clearly described, with sensible error-mitigation strategies (CoT prompting, smallest-mask selection, multi-view voting) that are individually ablated (Fig. 8).

Careful quality control: a 5K human-verified test split is constructed with documented inter-stage failure analysis (84.8% success rate) and a transparent breakdown of failure modes (Fig. 4), lending credibility to the benchmark's reliability.

Espresso-3D/2D provide a clean, symmetric architecture that isolates the dataset's contribution from model design, and pretraining consistently improves both Espresso and existing baselines (OpenAD, PointRefer, AffordanceNet) on unseen categories across both LASO and AGD20K, supporting the central claim that the dataset offers transferable supervision.

Thoughtful confound-control analyses: held-out-category filtering (Table 5) shows gains are not simply due to category leakage, pretraining-scale ablation (Table A3) shows monotonic improvement with data volume, and cross-domain asymmetry is decomposed into training-volume vs. class-coverage effects (Table A4).

Qualitative synthetic-to-real transfer to real robot manipulation scenes (Open X-Embodiment) and comparison against human annotations on 3D-AffordanceNet meshes (Fig. A2) provide additional, if informal, evidence of annotation quality and practical utility.
Good reproducibility support: detailed implementation appendix (model checkpoints, compute, hyperparameters, background augmentation ablation) facilitates replication.
weaknesses: Absolute performance on the Affogato-750K 3D test split is quite low even in-domain (best aIoU 13.6, Table 3), which could reflect either genuine task difficulty or substantial residual noise in the automatically generated 3D heatmaps that is not fully captured by the 84.8% human-rated "success" (a fairly coarse quality signal without reported inter-annotator agreement).

The object distribution is heavily skewed toward Daily-Used (121,799 of 150,104 objects), so the headline diversity numbers are somewhat concentrated in one subset; the class/affordance counts in Table 1 rely on VLM-predicted labels with ad hoc frequency thresholds (>10/>100), making the diversity comparison to other datasets not entirely apples-to-apples.

Benefits of pretraining are not uniform: PointRefer shows degraded seen-split performance after Affogato-750K pretraining (20.2 vs 20.8 aIoU, and drops in AUC/SIM), which is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed—it's unclear when/why pretraining can hurt in-domain performance.

Real-world generalization is only demonstrated qualitatively (Fig. 7); no quantitative benchmark on real images with ground truth is provided to substantiate the synthetic-to-real transfer claim beyond a few illustrative examples.

The annotation pipeline's reliance on rigid Objaverse meshes without articulation likely limits accuracy for affordances requiring state change (e.g., "open," "pull to turn on"), a limitation not explicitly analyzed despite such affordances appearing prominently in the query examples.

Espresso's architectural contribution is intentionally modest (assembled from existing pretrained encoders/decoders per prior work), which is appropriate given the dataset-centric framing but means the paper's novelty rests almost entirely on the data pipeline and dataset itself; this should be read as a Datasets/Benchmarks-type contribution rather than an algorithmic one, which the paper does not explicitly declare.
